extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent attorneys, in-house counsel, and judges interested in fee-shifting under 35 U.S.C. §285
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate whether a patent case qualifies as "exceptional" for an award of attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. §285 in light of the Supreme Court's Octane Fitness and Highmark decisions. The page analyzes the new, flexible standard and the kinds of factual and procedural conduct that may make a case "stand out."

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional case — "stands out" standard
rubrics_metrics.description: "An 'exceptional' case is simply one that stands out from others with respect to the substantive strength of a party's litigating position (considering both the governing law and the facts of the case) or the unreasonable manner in which the case was litigated." (Octane, slip op. at 7-8)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the Supreme Court's dictionary-based, flexible formulation replacing the Federal Circuit's rigid test. The Court emphasized a case-by-case assessment — the case must 'stand out' relative to others. Practitioners should evaluate both substantive legal/factual strength and litigation behavior; either dimension can make a case exceptional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive strength of a party's litigating position
rubrics_metrics.description: The court can look to the 'substantial strength' of a party's position, either legally or factually, when deciding whether a case stands out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key issues include whether asserting a (presumed valid) issued patent can ever be exceptional (e.g., when a patent holder overreaches), whether a questionable-but-presumed-valid patent could trigger fees, whether lack of invalidity counterclaims or objectively weak denials/defenses matter, and whether this prong is assessed at pleading or after adverse rulings. An adverse ruling that destroys a party's primary theory may later make its position 'substantially weak.' Consider Rule 11-like viability but remember Octane did not confine the inquiry to Rule 11 standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreasonable manner of litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: A case may be exceptional because of 'the unreasonable manner in which the case was litigated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and gray areas identified include discovery abuse, overzealous advocacy crossing a line, extensive motion practice, and refusal to settle. The conduct need not be independently sanctionable to support an exceptional finding, but it must 'stand out' compared with ordinary litigation. Trial courts must draw the line — routine zealous advocacy should not automatically trigger fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective bad faith or objectively baseless suits (either may suffice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court indicated that either subjective bad faith or an objectively baseless suit could be sufficient to find a case 'exceptional,' without requiring both as the Federal Circuit previously did.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This relaxes the Federal Circuit's two-prong Brooks Furniture test. Litigators should prepare arguments and evidence addressing either the party's state of mind (bad faith) or objective baselessness; proof of both is no longer required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation-related misconduct as a possible but non-exclusive basis
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit had previously categorized 'litigation-related misconduct' (e.g., willful infringement, fraud, inequitable conduct, Rule 11 violations) as bases for exceptional-case findings, but the Supreme Court noted those types of misconduct are 'otherwise, independently sanctionable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While such misconduct remains relevant, the Court rejected using them as the sole or exclusive benchmark. Courts may still find exceptional cases based on misconduct, but may also find fees where conduct is unreasonable yet not independently sanctionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary burden for fee-shifting under §285
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court held that §285 imposes no heightened evidentiary burden (i.e., no clear-and-convincing requirement) for an accused infringer seeking fees despite the presumption of patent validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit's approach (requiring clear and convincing evidence because patents are presumed valid) was rejected. Practitioners should note that courts have discretion in assessing the evidence, but there is no special statutory evidentiary hurdle imposed by §285 per Octane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-practicing entities and size-of-party considerations are not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Being a non-practicing entity (NPE) or the fact that a large company sues a smaller competitor does not inherently make a case 'exceptional.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-policy/sentiment against 'trolls' is not a substitute for the statutory standard. Stray internal statements (e.g., employees' emails) may be found immaterial if not connected to litigation. Courts will examine the record; mere status or size disparity alone will not automatically trigger fee awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal character of the exceptional-case inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions remain about when the 'stand out' inquiry should be made — at pleading, after discovery, or post-adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Octane leaves room for courts to consider how the case evolves; an initially plausible claim may become exceptional after adverse rulings, discovery disclosures, or other developments. Parties should preserve and develop factual records relevant to timing when contesting or seeking fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: District court discretion and flexible, case-by-case application
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court emphasized a flexible, totality-of-the-circumstances approach and remanded Octane for further proceedings consistent with its opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many open questions are left to trial courts. Practitioners should expect varied district-court applications and be prepared to present tailored factual and legal arguments to show whether a case 'stands out.' Use Octane as a framework but anticipate fact-specific outcomes.
